## Overview

Each case study this semester ended with a limitation stated out loud instead of
swept under the rug: CS 1's optimizer is only as trustworthy as an estimate of
$\boldsymbol{\mu}$ that Section 2 showed is genuinely hard to pin down. CS 2's
basket has a real, basket-wide edge, but it comes bundled with the crash risk
the lecture warned about from the start. CS 3's market maker has to be fast
enough to survive contact with latency and queue priority, and even then is
quoting under an assumption — driftless, Gaussian midprice moves — that the
real tape doesn't always honor. CS 4's hedge is built on a single volatility
that the market's own smile proves doesn't exist.

**The final project asks you to pick exactly one of these four open problems
and take a serious run at it.** Not a cosmetic extension — more tickers, a
longer backtest window, a nicer plot — but a focused piece of work whose whole
point is the difficulty itself: what would it actually take to estimate
$\boldsymbol{\mu}$ well enough to trust, to make carry survive its own crashes,
to make market making robust to speed and a changing market, or to hedge
honestly against a smile that a single $\sigma$ can't capture?

This is deliberately open-ended. Per the syllabus, the final project is "an
open-ended quantitative analysis of a financial question of your choosing,
ideally drawing on at least one case study methodology and its supporting
mathematical framework," presented live during the final class session, with
the detailed rubric posted on Canvas. This document exists to help you pick a
good question — specifically, to name the hard problem inside each case study
precisely enough that you can recognize whether your proposed project is
actually attacking it, or just circling it.

---

## The Open Problem in Each Case Study

Pick **one**. You are not required to have used that case study's exact data
or code as your starting point, but your project should engage with the
problem as stated below, not a watered-down version of it.

### Case Study 1 — Mean-Variance Portfolios: $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ Is the Bottleneck

Section 2 made the uncomfortable point as directly as possible: $\mathbf{w}^*
\propto \hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}$ needs
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}$, and $\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}$ is estimated so poorly,
at realistic sample sizes, that the "optimal" portfolio is often mostly noise
dressed up as a formula. $\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}$ is comparatively
well-behaved; $\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}$ is the genuine bottleneck. Having a
trustworthy $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ is exactly what would make mean-variance theory
live up to its promise — the theory was never the weak link, the input was.

A project here takes on the estimation problem directly: shrinkage toward a
structured target (Black-Litterman, James-Stein, a factor-implied prior),
robust or Bayesian estimation that explicitly represents estimation
uncertainty instead of plugging in a point estimate, a factor model that
estimates fewer, more stable quantities instead of $k$ noisy means, or a
robust/minimax formulation of the optimizer itself that hedges against
$\boldsymbol{\mu}$ being wrong. Whatever you choose, the project only counts
if you show — out-of-sample, against the plug-in sample-mean baseline from CS
1 — that your approach actually produces a more trustworthy
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}$ or a portfolio that is less damaged by
$\boldsymbol{\mu}$ risk.

### Case Study 2 — The Carry Basket: The Edge Is Real, the Drawdowns Are the Problem

Section 3's basket-wide Fama regressions confirmed the forward premium puzzle
holds across G10, not just for one lucky pair — the carry edge is not a
fluke. But Section 5 also made unavoidable what the literature has always
said about carry: it is "picking up nickels in front of a steamroller,"
negatively skewed, prone to sudden, correlated unwinds (2008, the SNB peg
break, the August 2024 JPY unwind). The idea is sound; what carry actually
needs is a way to keep collecting the differential without being destroyed
the one time in twenty the trade unwinds all at once. CS 2's own Section 6
bonus (a trend filter) was one modest attempt at this — the final project is
the chance to take that problem seriously rather than as an optional add-on.

A project here builds and honestly evaluates a real defense against carry's
tail risk: a regime-detection overlay that de-risks ahead of (or quickly
after) a crash signal, a volatility- or correlation-based dynamic leverage
rule, an explicit options-based tail hedge (and its cost), or a systematic
comparison of several such defenses against more crash episodes than CS 2's
original window covered. The bar for success is explicit: does your defense
measurably improve the basket's skewness, max drawdown, or crash-episode
behavior, and how much of the average carry return did you give up to get
that improvement?

### Case Study 3 — Market Making: Fast Enough, and Right About the Market

CS 3 split the head trader's question into frictions (fees, latency, queue
priority, adverse selection) and showed each one eats into a zero-friction
backtest's P&L. But there's a second, deeper issue underneath "can you be
fast enough": the Avellaneda-Stoikov policy itself assumes the midprice moves
like driftless Brownian motion. Real tape doesn't always cooperate — trends,
news, regime shifts, and the very "toxic" windows Section 6's markout
analysis is built to detect are all departures from that assumption. Being
fast enough to execute the policy and having a policy that still makes sense
once the market stops being driftless Brownian motion are two different
problems, and CS 3 left the second one almost entirely unaddressed.

A project here goes after either side, or both: deepen the microstructure
realism (a better queue-position model, latency compensation that adapts
rather than just measures the damage, adverse-selection-aware order sizing),
or relax the driftless-Brownian-motion assumption directly — a
regime-switching or jump-aware reservation price, a trend/momentum-adjusted
midprice forecast feeding into the AS formula, or a toxicity-aware rule
(building on CS 3 Section 8's suggestion) that widens or steps aside during
exactly the windows your markout analysis flags. Show, on the real tape, that
your version holds up where the baseline AS policy would have gotten picked
off or priced out.

### Case Study 4 — Options Hedging: One $\sigma$ Can't Describe the Market

CS 4 Sections 3 and 6 demonstrated the smile is not a synthetic artifact — a
real SPX chain genuinely cannot be matched by one Black-Scholes $\sigma$
across every strike, and Section 4's two-$\sigma$ comparison showed that
mismatch isn't academic: a hedger whose $\sigma$ doesn't match the market's
own view carries real, quantifiable Vega exposure that a delta-only hedge
never touches, by construction, no matter how often you rebalance or how
carefully you account for transaction costs. Black-Scholes is useful; it is
also, provably on your own data, wrong in a specific and structural way, and
a delta-only hedge leaves exactly that wrongness unmanaged.

A project here either fixes the pricing side or the hedging side of that gap.
On pricing: calibrate a genuinely smile-consistent model to your real chain
(local volatility, a simple stochastic-volatility model like SABR, or a
jump-diffusion model) and show it prices away-from-the-money strikes
meaningfully better than a flat-$\sigma$ Black-Scholes fit, out of sample
across your data window. On hedging: build the Vega-neutral, two-option hedge
that CS 4 Section 8 only sketched, and quantify — on a real historical path,
not just a simulated one — how much hedging-P&L variance it removes relative
to the delta-only hedge from Section 4/5, and at what transaction-cost
tradeoff.

## What Counts as Embellishment (and What Doesn't)

**Not acceptable:** re-running your chosen case study's existing sections
with a longer window, more tickers, or a different random seed. That's
repetition, not research.

**Acceptable:** a focused attack on the specific difficulty named above, with
its own well-defined baseline (almost always: the relevant case study's own
original approach), its own comparison, and an honest verdict on whether your
idea actually worked — including the real possibility that it didn't, or
that it helped less than you expected. A project that tries something
reasonable and reports "this didn't actually fix the problem, and here's
why" is worth more than one that quietly cherry-picks a flattering result.

You do not need to reuse your original case study's code verbatim, and you
are welcome to pull additional data if your chosen direction needs it — just
document your pipeline and caching with the same rigor CS 1–4 required.

## Deliverables

Per the syllabus: a written report and a live presentation during the final
class session. Hold yourself to the same standards the case studies did —
reproducible code, an explicit accounting of frictions and uncertainty where
relevant, honestly labeled figures, and a closing recommendation paragraph
addressed to whichever stakeholder (PM, head trader, desk head) your chosen
case study's scenario was written for. The detailed rubric is posted on
Github.
